newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Australian sugar faces tough yr-QSC.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Australian sugar faces tough yr-QSC.

text.p: Queensland Sugar Corp (QSC) has "very substantially sold and priced" its big 1996 crop and hopes to break into the Indonesian and Saudi Arabian markets this year but views falling world sugar prices with concern, chief executive David Rutledge said on Monday.

"We're looking at an eight to 10 percent increase in production and maybe an eight to 10 percent reduction in price. It looks at the moment as though (QSC's) gross revenues are going to be relatively unchanged," he said in an interview.
"That's not good news for the industry," he told Reuters.
Falling prices in the past year were a disappointment and the trend had continued since then, he said.
"That's something of a concern for the industry. We're looking at quite a reasonable drop in prices again for the 1996/97 year," he said.
Rutledge said he was not prepared to say how far world prices might drop in 1997. "No one knows."
But QSC's pool prices were expected to be eight to 10 percent lower than in 1995/96, he said.
And world surpluses were continuing, while competition from Thailand was "fearsome" and Brazil and South Africa were both selling into the Asian region, he said.
If forecast surpluses for the next year or so were realised they would keep a lot of downward pressure on price, he said.
Rutledge was speaking after the release of QSC's annual report for the year ended June 30.
Only a genuinely new development, through crop failure or a new demand initiative, would turn the market around, he said.

QSC would increase sales in the current year through increased raw sugar production, currently expected to be a record of 5.0 million tonnes for Queensland and 5.3 million tonnes for Australia as a whole.
But with falling world prices, it was still too early to say how QSC's revenues would emerge, he said.
In the latest year, QSC's sugar sales revenue declined to A$1.994 billion from A$2.051 billion after a 4.6 percent decrease in exports to 3.79 million tonnes.
QSC's primary attention was now on the 1997 crop with the current crop was "very substantially sold and priced", he said.
While insulated to some extent from falling market prices, sales had been struck when prices were not particularly attractive, he said.
On 1997 sales prospects, Rutledge said a new refinery to come on stream in Indonesia in 1996/97 raised some prospect of first Australian raw sugar sales, from the 1996 crop.
"We'll just have to see," he said. Possible tonnages to Indonesia would not be as big as in the Middle East.
QSC also could be selling 1996 crop raw sugar to Saudi Arabia for the first time to supply the approximately half-million tonnes a year refinery coming on stream this year.
While 1996 crop sales to Saudi Arabia might not be substantial, QSC hoped for a longer-term good market share.
The reduction in QSC's sales to China in the latest year, to 355,000 tonnes from 638,000 tonnes, reflected lower import demand after the 1994/95 import "binge", he said.
The drop in QSC's 1995/96 sales to Singapore, to 80,000 tonnes from 166,000 tonnes, was primarily the result of increased competition from Thailand and South Africa, he said.
There was a reasonably widespread view that China next year would import substantially more. "We would probably expect to get our share of that," he said.
There was also some prospect of Australia's share of the Singapore market returning to more historical levels but that would greatly depend on market competition, he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
